title: Europe’s China Strategy Is Ready for a Refresh
gist: France and Germany jointly named China as 'challenging our economy' for the first time in July 2026 and the European Council has mandated new trade defense instruments, but the author argues Brussels' subsidy-and-overcapacity framing misses that CCP human rights abuses are structurally fused with Chinese industrial competitiveness. Beijing is now externalizing its coercive legal apparatus onto European firms through decrees that block supply-chain transparency and forced-labor risk identification.

insights.claim: At the Franco-German Ministerial Council on July 16-17, 2026, France and Germany for the first time after years of division jointly identified China as 'challenging our economy' and called for an EU roadmap to protect European industries from Chinese competition.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: The Paris-Berlin split was the main brake on EU trade defense against China; its removal raises the probability of binding EU-wide measures on Chinese imports.
insights.quote: called for the establishment of an EU roadmap to protect European industries against Chinese competition
insights.locator: At the Franco-German Ministerial Council on July 16-17

insights.claim: The European Council on June 19, 2026 gave the European Commission a clear mandate to develop additional trade defense instruments against subsidized imports, adding to existing safeguard, anti-dumping and anti-subsidy duty tools.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: A concrete legislative pipeline for new EU import barriers is now open — sectors exposed to Chinese overcapacity face rising European tariff risk.
insights.locator: At the European Council on June 19

themes.theme: Human rights as an economic variable, not a side issue

insights.claim: State-imposed forced labor, Uyghur labor transfers, the ban on independent unions, and coerced relocations feature in exactly the Chinese industries most central to Europe's trade relationship — electric battery production, solar and renewable energy supply chains, and technology.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: EU battery and solar import chains carry latent legal exposure that trade-defense tariffs do not address; forced-labor enforcement is a separate and potentially sharper supply-chain risk.
insights.quote: China’s economy and industry are intertwined with the Chinese government’s human rights abuses
insights.locator: The truth is that China's economy and industry

insights.claim: European governments deliberately tolerated Chinese human rights violations because strategic sectors including automotive and critical raw materials for electronics and batteries depended on access to Chinese markets and suppliers.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: The tolerance was economically motivated, so it will only reverse where substitution is feasible — expect enforcement to lag most in critical raw materials.
insights.quote: European governments have, in effect, turned a blind eye to these human rights violations as some of Europe’s most important industries sought access to Chinese markets and Chinese suppliers.
insights.locator: European governments have, in effect, turned a blind eye

insights.claim: As long as the EU isolates human rights from trade, procurement, industrial policy, and security, it will systematically underestimate the nature of the China challenge because the Commission's trade defense tools do not address the structural fusion of the CCP's authoritarian model with its economic policy.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: Anti-dumping duties treat a symptom; if this framing wins in Brussels, the policy toolkit widens from tariffs to sanctions, procurement bans and due diligence enforcement.
insights.quote: As long as the EU isolates human rights from trade, procurement, industrial policy, and security, it will keep underestimating the nature of the challenge.
insights.locator: But the Commission proposals do not address

insights.claim: Beijing has passed new decrees specifically designed to prevent foreign companies from pressing for supply-chain transparency or identifying forced-labor risks, including blocking foreign firms that try to stop sourcing from Chinese suppliers linked to abuses.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: European corporates face a direct legal conflict — Chinese law now penalizes the very due diligence EU law will require, creating unavoidable compliance jeopardy.
insights.quote: trying to block foreign companies that try to stop sourcing from Chinese suppliers linked to human rights abuses
insights.locator: In addition to existing laws restricting cross-border transfer

insights.claim: Chinese coercive practices that once targeted domestic lawyers, activists and political opponents are increasingly being aimed at foreign companies and their staff through extraterritorial measures.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: Personnel and detention risk for foreign staff in China is escalating from a tail risk to an operating-environment feature; reprice China-exposed operational footprints.
insights.quote: The Chinese Communist Party’s coercive logic is no longer contained within China’s borders: it is being externalized to the operating environment of European firms.
insights.locator: Furthermore, Beijing has now made it harder

insights.claim: The author calls for the EU forced labor products regulation to be strengthened to permit region-wide bans on goods made through state-imposed forced labor in Xinjiang or through labor transfers, rather than case-by-case determinations.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: A region-wide Xinjiang ban would function like the US UFLPA rebuttable presumption and would hit solar polysilicon and battery inputs hardest.
insights.locator: In particular, they should strengthen the EU regulation

insights.claim: Robust enforcement of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive would simultaneously bind Chinese companies operating in Europe and force European firms to police their Chinese suppliers.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: CSDDD enforcement intensity is the practical transmission channel from EU human rights policy to corporate supply-chain cost — watch it as a compliance-cost input.
insights.locator: By robustly enforcing human rights due diligence legislation

insights.claim: The author argues EU states must harmonize their China policies jointly precisely so they can withstand Chinese retaliation, implying that unilateral national action invites targeted economic punishment.
insights.speaker: Hélène de Rengervé
insights.so_what: Retaliation risk is the binding constraint on EU China policy; the degree of member-state coordination is the best predictor of how far measures actually go.
insights.quote: They should work jointly to harmonize their policies, so that together, they can resist the Chinese government’s retaliation
insights.locator: The Chinese government's human rights abuses should not be isolated
